knowledge_point.title: Solving for One Coefficient in a Linear Combination

question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the properties of addition/subtraction and scalar multiplication of vectors to isolate the $k$ term, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2} & =0 \\ 4\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+k\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-4\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\ k\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the first components, we get

$$
4k=-8\,⟹\,k=-2.
$$

But then

$$
\begin{aligned}-2\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}\ne \begin{bmatrix}-8 \\ -16\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there is no $k$ such that $4{a}_{1}+k{a}_{2}=0.$
